# Machine file v2 fixtures — provenance

**These files were produced by the Tamga API server's own encoder. They were
not written by hand and not produced by this SDK.**

Every `.machine` file here is the output of `encode_machine_file`
(`tamga-api`, `src/shared/crypto/machine_file.rs`) — the same function that
builds the `certificate` string a real `POST /machines/{id}/actions/check-out`
returns. `manifest.json` carries the signing key material and checkout
parameters the server used, one entry per file.

## Why this matters

Before these landed, every machine-file test in this SDK verified a file this
SDK had built itself, through `test/helpers/checkoutFixtures.ts`. A fixture
builder that mirrors the verifier's misreading of the wire format produces a
green suite over a verifier that cannot open anything the server emits. That
is exactly what happened here, and it hid four separate defects for two
years — the missing `+v2` marker, the dot-separated encrypted `enc`, the
unenforced `meta.exp`, and (found while wiring these up) an ECDSA
verification that never hashed the message.

**Do not add a fixture generated by this repository to this directory.** If a
case is missing, ask for it to be produced from the server's encoder.

## Contents

12 fixtures: 4 signing schemes × 3 variants.

| scheme | `alg` (plain) | `alg` (encrypted) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ED25519_SIGN` | `base64+ed25519+v2` | `aes-256-gcm+ed25519+v2` |
| `ECDSA_P256_SIGN` | `base64+ecdsa-p256+v2` | `aes-256-gcm+ecdsa-p256+v2` |
| `RSA_2048_PKCS1_SIGN` | `base64+rsa-sha256+v2` | `aes-256-gcm+rsa-sha256+v2` |
| `RSA_2048_PKCS1_PSS_SIGN` | `base64+rsa-pss-sha256+v2` | `aes-256-gcm+rsa-pss-sha256+v2` |

Variants per scheme: `*_plain_valid`, `*_encrypted_valid`, `*_plain_expired`.

## `manifest.json`

A flat object keyed by fixture name. Tests iterate it rather than naming
files, so a fixture added to this directory is picked up with no test edit.

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file` | file name in this directory |
| `alg` | the `alg` string inside the certificate |
| `encrypted` | whether the payload is AES-256-GCM encrypted |
| `enc_is_dot_separated` | whether `enc` is `"<nonce_b64>.<cipher_b64>"` |
| `public_key_b64` | the account's public key for `scheme` (see the note below) |
| `kid` | the `meta.kid` claim inside the signed payload |
| `license_key` | HKDF ikm for an encrypted file, `null` when plain |
| `fingerprint` | HKDF info — the machine the file is bound to |
| `expired` | whether `meta.exp` is in the past relative to `meta.iat` |
| `scheme` | the server's `LicenseScheme` **Rust variant name**, e.g. `Ed25519Sign` — map it to the SDK's wire literal (`ED25519_SIGN`) before passing it in |

### `public_key_b64` encodings

Taken verbatim from the server's account key material, so the encoding is
whatever the server publishes, per scheme:

- `Ed25519Sign` — 32-byte raw public key.
- `EcdsaP256Sign` — 65-byte uncompressed P-256 point (`0x04 ‖ X ‖ Y`).
- `Rsa2048Pkcs1Sign` / `Rsa2048Pkcs1PssSign` — **270-byte PKCS#1
  `RSAPublicKey` DER**, not SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The server's own doc
  comments (`key_material.rs:37`, `license_signing.rs:142`) call this SPKI and
  are wrong; `aws-lc-rs`'s `RsaKeyPair::public_key()` hands back PKCS#1, and
  the server's `rsa_public_key_is_spki_der` test only asserts `len > 256`,
  which a 270-byte PKCS#1 blob also satisfies. `src/crypto/rsa.ts` accepts
  both encodings for exactly this reason.

## Time-dependence

`meta.iat` is the moment the fixture was minted and `meta.exp` is
`iat ± 3600`. A test that compares against the wall clock would pass today and
start failing an hour after these were generated, so the suite anchors its
reference clock to each file's own signed `iat` claim instead
(`test/machine-file-server-fixtures.spec.ts`).
